The '''Yinggarda language''' (also written '''Yingkarta''' and '''Inggarda''') is an [[Australian Aboriginal languages|Australian Aboriginal language]]. It is an [[endangered language]], but efforts at [[language revival]] are being made.

==Name==
"Yinggarda" has been spelt in a number of ways, some linguists (including Dench) writing it as "Yingkarta".

== Classification ==
It is one of the [[Kartu languages]] of the [[Pama–Nyungan languages|Pama–Nyungan family]]. The ''[[Ethnologue]]'' equates Yinggarda with Pulinya<ref name=AIATSISW43>{{cite web|url=https://collection.aiatsis.gov.au/austlang/language/w43|website=Austlang|publisher=AIATSIS|title=W43: Pulinya|date=26 July 2019 |access-date=14 January 2020}}</ref> but it is unclear what the basis is for this connection as [[Wilfrid Douglas]], who recorded the name 'Pulinya,' described it as a name for the old [[Geraldton]] language.{{Specify|date=May 2024}}

== Geographic distribution ==
[[File:Australia Western Australia location map.svg|thumb]]
Yinggarda country is around [[Carnarvon, Western Australia|Carnarvon]], on the central western coast of Western Australia, and extends inland to near [[Gascoyne Junction]] and south to around the mouth of the [[Wooramel River]].

==Dialects==
Maya (Maia), known only from 12 names of totem species identical to those in Yinggarda (e.g. {{Lang|yia|yalipirri}} 'emu' and {{Lang|yia|wura}} 'dog'), is reported to have been "like" Yinggarda and may have been a dialect.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Austin |first=Peter |date=30 June 1988 |title=Aboriginal languages of the Gascoyne-Ashburton region |url=https://opal.latrobe.edu.au/articles/journal_contribution/Aboriginal_languages_of_the_Cascoyne-Ashburton_region/22201855 |pages= |doi=10.26181/22201855|journal=Working Papers in Linguistics}}</ref>

== Language revival ==
A dictionary of Yinggarda by [[Peter Austin (linguist)|Peter K. Austin]] was published in 1992. A sketch [[linguistic description|grammar]] was written by Alan Dench in 1998, who worked with some of the last speakers and carried out his research mainly in the 1970s and 1980s.<ref name=":0" /> The Yamaji Language Centre, now  the [[Irra Wangga Language Centre]], has been continuing to work on the Yinggarda language since 1993.<ref>{{cite web |title=Irra Wangga Language Centre: Mid West languages: Yingkarta |url=http://www.bundiyarra.com.au/index.php?page=mid_west_languages#section8 |access-date=14 January 2020 |website=Bundiyarra Aboriginal Community Aboriginal Corporation}}</ref>

{{as of|2020}}, Yinggarda is one of 20 languages prioritised as part of the Priority Languages Support Project, being undertaken by First Languages Australia and funded by the [[Department of Communications and the Arts]]. The project aims to "identify and document critically-endangered languages — those languages for which little or no documentation exists, where no recordings have previously been made, but where there are living speakers".<ref>{{cite web |title=Priority Languages Support Project |url=https://www.firstlanguages.org.au/projects/plsp |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200113071114/https://www.firstlanguages.org.au/projects/plsp |archive-date=13 January 2020 |access-date=13 January 2020 |website=First Languages Australia}}</ref>

* The alveolar rhotic is realized as a "very lax" tap {{IPA|[ɾ]}} between vowels, often similar to an alveolar approximant {{IPA|[ɹ]}} in quality. It also becomes a trill {{IPA|[r]}} before consonants, and is often heard as a stop {{IPA|[d]}}.
* Stops /k, t̪, ʈ/ are heard as [ɣ, ð, ɽ] when in intervocalic position.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Dench |first=Alan C. |title=Yingkarta |publisher=Munich: München: Lincom Europa |year=1998}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=12}}
